articles.body: The "100% Dart" Myth in Production Mobile Engineering One of the most common architectural mistakes teams make when adopting Flutter is assuming that every feature should be written purely in Dart. While Flutter's rendering engine and pub.dev ecosystem handle 90% of standard CRUD and UI workflows effortlessly, forcing high-frequency hardware interactions—such as raw stylus ink prediction, custom WebRTC media tracks, or USB serial communication—through pure Dart abstractions often introduces unacceptable latency. Where Pure Dart Hits a Bottleneck In a recent interactive whiteboard project deployed on large Android touch panels, relying purely on standard Flutter gesture arenas resulted in a noticeable 70.7ms stylus stroke lag. Why?

articles.body: Over the past few weeks, I built and shipped 8 production cloud scrapers on the Apify Store alongside two cross-browser Manifest V3 extensions on the Mozilla Add-ons Store. Most scraping tutorials default to spinning up full headless Chromium instances for every URL. While Playwright and Puppeteer are essential when dealing with heavy client-side hydration, they are often overkill for structured B2B extraction, e-commerce catalog indexing, and technical SEO auditing. By combining CheerioCrawler in Crawlee with hidden platform JSON endpoints and regex-backed DOM parsers, you can cut memory overhead and runtime costs by over 85%. Here is a practical look at the architecture behind these tools and where you can try them out. 1.

articles.title: How to test if an AI agent can find your pricing page (Playwright, no LLM)
articles.excerpt: If you want to know whether an AI agent can get from your homepage to your prices, you can check most of it with a plain Playwright script and no model at all. The script looks for a link whose access…
articles.body: If you want to know whether an AI agent can get from your homepage to your prices, you can check most of it with a plain Playwright script and no model at all. The script looks for a link whose accessible name contains "Pricing", clicks it, waits for a price to render, and reads the prices from the page text. If any step fails, a browser agent driving your site through the accessibility tree or the DOM will probably struggle at the same spot. I ran a first version of this on five browser-infrastructure sites today (Steel, Browser Use, Anchor Browser, Hyperbrowser and Browserless). All five passed. The script itself failed three times before it gave honest answers, and those failures are the useful part of this post.

articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built Slothshot is a sloth that names my screenshots while I sleep, on my own laptop, and doesn't stop until the job is done, even when the laptop dies halfway through. My Screenshots folder is where useful things go to be forgotten, because every boarding pass and Wi-Fi password I have ever needed lands there under a name like Screenshot 2026-10-19 105126.png , and on the day I need one again I spend five minutes squinting at thumbnails that all look the same. Slothshot does the tidying for me overnight, slowly and steadily, with open models that never leave my machine. It reads every screenshot. RapidOCR, an open OCR model running in ONNX Runtime, pulls the text off each image.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 25, 1671: Astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovers Iapetus, Saturn's 'yin-yang' moon
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Iapetus was the second moon anyone had ever found orbiting Saturn, and it was the first of four moons Cassini would discover at the ringed planet. The Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens had discovered Titan , the largest of Saturn's moons, about six years earlier. After Cassini found Iapetus, he also found the moons Rhea, Tethys and Dione. When Cassini first saw Iapetus, the moon looked like a tiny speck on the west side of Saturn. He calculated its orbit and thought he would be able to see it again on the east side of Saturn 39 days later, but it was nowhere to be seen.

articles.body: On Episode 233 of This Week In Space , Tariq Malik and guest host Rick Jenet are joined by Dr. Amanda Smith-Hackler, the Director of Education for the Universities Space Research Association and Principal Investigator for the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) Scholars and STEM Workforce Development Programs, about the new and exciting opportunities available to young people seeking to enter the space workforce. Newspace is hiring! articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.
